newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Costain plunges deeper into red.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Costain plunges deeper into red.

text.p: Costain Group Plc, the British builder which clinched a last-ditch survival refinancing this summer, plunged deeper into the red in its first half results but told investors that things would improve by the year end.

Losses swelled to 19.2 million pounds ($30 million) in the six months to June 30, from 10.4 million last year. Again there was no dividend payout, but Allan Lovell, chief executive, said the full year results would be "considerably better" than 1995.
Costain predicts higher turnover and profits by the close of the year, after interim sales fell to 360 from 458 million.
The construction-to-engineering group was on the brink of administrative receivership this summer when Costain told investors that a 73 million pounds refinancing was its last chance for survival.

Lovell said Costain was now restored to financial health after turning in one of the worst performances in the stock market in recent years. Shares are currently flat at 59 pence - a far cry from the value of 14 pounds apiece five years ago.
The chief executive cited a number of reasons for his optimisim despite an interim report which said trading conditions remained little changed and saw losses deepen across all divisions.
First, construction turnover in the six months to June 30 had been "well below the trend". But he said it would improve significantly in the second half to "over 300 million (pounds)" in sales.
"This is a key issue. And it's not just the amount (of business) but the quality."
Year-end results would also be boosted by the fact that there "will not be any write-offs - this will make them hugely better." Lower debt levels should also help.
But despite his high hopes, Lovell refused to be drawn on when the company will start paying dividends to investors again.
He said he had a timeframe in mind but "I'm not setting myself up as a hostage to fortune."
Costain's string of disposals is almost complete except for U.S. Coal. But Lovell said it was in talks with a possible buyer.
He also said that the future strategy hinged on expanding overseas sales, using Costain's three biggest investors as a springboard into the South East Asia and Middle East markets.
The three biggest shareholders - Intria of Malaysia ACID.KL, M.A. Kharafi and Sons of Kuwait and Raymond International of Saudi Arabia - own a total of 75 percent of the shares.
It expects Intria to help it gain small contracts in the next six months and a stake in a larger project next year.
Costain aims to have the largest proportion of its business stemming from overseas markets in the years ahead.

Looking at a breakdown of the results in the first half, engineering and construction made a loss of five million pounds, down from its 2.1 million loss on turnover of 251 million pounds versus 319 million.

U.S. Coal reported a loss of 2.8 million pounds versus a profit of 700,000 as sales fell to 5.2 million tons from 5.7 million tons. Property saw a loss of 2.4 million pounds, down from 1.4 million. ($1=.6415 Pound)
